{{DISPLAYTITLE:Propositional equality}}
{{Plebeian|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Two kinds of equality}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

'''Propositional equality''' is the proposition <code>a = b</code>. A proof of it is a term
of that type, built and used like any other proof. It is distinct from
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Definitional equality|definitional equality]], which is a
judgment the checker tests by computation and which no term records. Lean defines
propositional equality as an inductive family with a single constructor. Symmetry,
transitivity, substitution and congruence are all derived from its eliminator. Function
extensionality is a theorem, proved from quotient types. Uniqueness of identity proofs
holds with no axiom at all.

== Equality as an inductive family ==

Lean's core library defines <code>Eq</code> as an inductive type in <code>Prop</code> with
one constructor, <code>Eq.refl</code>.<ref name="prelude">Lean 4 source, file <code>src/Init/Prelude.lean</code>, version 4.34.1: the definitions of <code>Eq</code>, <code>HEq</code>, <code>cast</code>, <code>congrArg</code>, <code>congr</code>, <code>congrFun</code> and <code>funext</code>, with their documentation comments. Apache License 2.0. https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/blob/v4.34.1/src/Init/Prelude.lean</ref> Lean prints it so:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#print Eq
example : 2 + 2 = 4 := rfl
</pre>
<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
inductive Eq.{u_1} : {α : Sort u_1} → α → α → Prop
number of parameters: 2
constructors:
Eq.refl : ∀ {α : Sort u_1} (a : α), a = a
</pre>

The two parameters are the type <code>α</code> and the left-hand side <code>a</code>. The
right-hand side is an '''index''': it varies between the type and the constructor's result,
and the constructor fixes it to <code>a</code>. The constructor alone therefore proves only
statements of the form <code>a = a</code>; every other equation needs an argument that ends
in one. Written as rules, formation and introduction are

:<math>\frac{\Gamma \vdash A : \mathrm{Sort}\,u \quad \Gamma \vdash a : A \quad \Gamma \vdash b : A}{\Gamma \vdash a = b : \mathrm{Prop}} \qquad \frac{\Gamma \vdash a : A}{\Gamma \vdash \mathrm{Eq.refl}\,a : a = a}</math>

The term <code>rfl</code> is <code>Eq.refl</code> with its argument left implicit. The
example <code>2 + 2 = 4 := rfl</code> is accepted because the checker finds
<code>2 + 2</code> and <code>4</code> definitionally equal; <code>rfl</code> then has the
type the statement asks for. Every proof by <code>rfl</code> is a definitional equality
packaged as a propositional one. Not every propositional equality is definitional: most
equations in mathematics need an argument, because no amount of computation turns one side
into the other.

== The eliminator ==

The recursor that [[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Inductive types and recursors|every inductive type receives]]
is, for <code>Eq</code>, the principle that makes equality useful.

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
set_option pp.proofs true in
#check @Eq.rec
</pre>
<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
@Eq.rec : {α : Sort u_2} →
  {a : α} → {motive : (a_1 : α) → a = a_1 → Sort u_1} → motive a (Eq.refl a) → {a_1 : α} → (t : a = a_1) → motive a_1 t
</pre>

The motive, written <math>C</math> below, is a family over every right-hand side <code>y</code> and every
proof that <code>a = y</code>. To produce an element of <code>C b h</code> it suffices to
produce one at the constructor, <code>C a (Eq.refl a)</code>:

:<math>\frac{\Gamma \vdash C : \Pi (y : A).\, a = y \to \mathrm{Sort}\,v \quad \Gamma \vdash c : C\,a\,(\mathrm{Eq.refl}\,a) \quad \Gamma \vdash h : a = b}{\Gamma \vdash \mathrm{Eq.rec}\,c\,h : C\,b\,h}</math>

with the computation rule

:<math>\mathrm{Eq.rec}\,c\,(\mathrm{Eq.refl}\,a) \equiv c</math>

'''The motive may land in any universe, not only in <code>Prop</code>.''' A proof of an
equation can therefore change the type of a piece of data. This is unusual for a
proposition: Lean permits it only because <code>Eq</code> passes the test for subsingleton
elimination, which is the subject of
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Proof irrelevance and subsingleton elimination|proof irrelevance and subsingleton elimination]].<ref name="refman-ind">''The Lean Language Reference'', version 4.34.0, §4.4 "Inductive Types", subsection "Subsingleton Elimination" (the recursor of <code>Eq</code>). https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/Inductive-Types/#subsingleton-elimination</ref>

== Transport ==

Applying the eliminator with a motive that does not depend on the proof gives
'''transport''': from <code>h : a = b</code> and a term whose type mentions <code>a</code>,
obtain the same term at <code>b</code>. Lean's core library defines <code>Eq.subst</code>
and <code>cast</code> this way.<ref name="prelude" /> The triangle <code>h ▸ e</code> is a
macro over <code>Eq.rec</code> and <code>Eq.symm</code>: it tries both orientations of
<code>h</code>, and rewrites the expected type when there is one, otherwise the type of
<code>e</code>.<ref name="parser">Lean 4 source, file <code>src/Lean/Parser/Term.lean</code>, version 4.34.1: the documentation comment of the <code>h ▸ e</code> syntax. Apache License 2.0. https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/blob/v4.34.1/src/Lean/Parser/Term.lean</ref> With it the familiar laws of equality are one line
each:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem symm' {α : Sort u} {a b : α} (h : a = b) : b = a :=
  h ▸ rfl

theorem trans' {α : Sort u} {a b c : α} (h₁ : a = b) (h₂ : b = c) : a = c :=
  h₂ ▸ h₁

theorem subst' {α : Sort u} {a b : α} (p : α → Prop) (h : a = b) (ha : p a) : p b :=
  h ▸ ha

theorem congrArg' {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} {a₁ a₂ : α} (f : α → β) (h : a₁ = a₂) :
    f a₁ = f a₂ :=
  h ▸ rfl

def castAlong {α β : Type} (h : α = β) (x : α) : β :=
  h ▸ x

#print axioms trans'
</pre>

The last command prints <code>'trans'' does not depend on any axioms</code>. Nothing beyond
the inductive definition is used. The definition <code>castAlong</code> is the case that
needs the large motive: its result is data of type <code>β</code>, obtained from data of
type <code>α</code> by a proof that the two types are equal.

== Congruence ==

The theorem <code>congrArg</code> above is the first congruence principle: equal arguments
give equal values. The core library adds <code>congrFun</code> (equal functions give equal
values at one argument) and <code>congr</code> (both at once), each proved by transport in
the same way. The library's documentation notes that tactics such as <code>congr</code>
and <code>simp</code> use <code>congrArg</code> internally to apply equalities inside
subterms.<ref name="prelude" /> <code>congrArg</code> and <code>congr</code> are stated for non-dependent functions. When the type of the
result depends on the argument, <code>f a₁</code> and <code>f a₂</code> have different
types, and the statement <code>f a₁ = f a₂</code> cannot even be formed. That case needs a
different relation.

== Heterogeneous equality ==

'''Heterogeneous equality''' relates terms whose types are not known to be definitionally
equal. It is a second inductive family, written <code>a ≍ b</code> in Lean 4.34.1:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#print HEq
#check fun (n m : Nat) (x : Fin (n + m)) (y : Fin (m + n)) => x ≍ y
#check @type_eq_of_heq
#check @eq_of_heq
</pre>
<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
inductive HEq.{u} : {α : Sort u} → α → {β : Sort u} → β → Prop
number of parameters: 2
constructors:
HEq.refl : ∀ {α : Sort u} (a : α), a ≍ a
fun n m x y => x ≍ y : (n m : Nat) → Fin (n + m) → Fin (m + n) → Prop
@type_eq_of_heq : ∀ {α β : Sort u_1} {a : α} {b : β}, a ≍ b → α = β
@eq_of_heq : ∀ {α : Sort u_1} {a a' : α}, a ≍ a' → a = a'
</pre>

The statement <code>x ≍ y</code> is well formed even though <code>Fin (n + m)</code> and
<code>Fin (m + n)</code> are equal only by a theorem about addition. The same statement
with <code>=</code> is rejected:

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#check fun (n m : Nat) (x : Fin (n + m)) (y : Fin (m + n)) => x = y
</pre>

Lean reports <code>Type mismatch</code>: <code>y</code> has type <code>Fin (m + n)</code> but
is expected to have type <code>Fin (n + m)</code>. A proof of <code>x ≍ y</code> carries a
proof that the types agree, which <code>type_eq_of_heq</code> extracts, and at a single type
it collapses to ordinary equality by <code>eq_of_heq</code>. The core library's own
documentation advises avoiding <code>HEq</code> where possible: the analogue of
<code>congr</code> fails for it, since from <code>f ≍ g</code> and <code>x ≍ y</code> it does
not follow that <code>f x ≍ g y</code>; the equality of types that <code>HEq</code> carries is
often too weak.<ref name="prelude" />

== Function extensionality ==

'''Function extensionality''' says that functions which agree at every argument are equal.
The eliminator of <code>Eq</code> offers no way to compare two lambda terms by their
values. The Lean reference manual notes that function extensionality would have to be an
axiom in Lean, were it not for quotient types, whose lifting operator has a definitional
computation rule.<ref name="refman-quot">''The Lean Language Reference'', version 4.34.0, §4.5.6 "Quotients and Function Extensionality". https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#quotient-funext</ref> The proof in the
core library forms the quotient of the function type by pointwise equality and applies each
class to an argument:<ref name="prelude" />

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem funext' {α : Sort u} {β : α → Sort v} {f g : (x : α) → β x}
    (h : ∀ x, f x = g x) : f = g :=
  let eqv (f g : (x : α) → β x) : Prop := ∀ x, f x = g x
  let app (q : Quot eqv) (x : α) : β x := Quot.lift (fun f => f x) (fun _ _ h => h x) q
  congrArg app (Quot.sound h)

#print axioms funext'
#print axioms funext
</pre>
<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
'funext'' depends on axioms: [Quot.sound]
'funext' depends on axioms: [Quot.sound]
</pre>

The axiom <code>Quot.sound</code> makes the classes of <code>f</code> and <code>g</code>
equal, and <code>congrArg</code> carries that equality through <code>app</code>. The proof
type-checks only because <code>app (Quot.mk eqv f)</code> reduces, by the computation rule
for <code>Quot.lift</code>, to <code>fun x => f x</code>, which is <code>f</code> up to
η. A merely propositional computation rule would not do: rewriting under the binder would
already need function extensionality.<ref name="refman-quot" /> The axiom itself, and why
it is one, are on [[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/The three axioms|the three axioms]].

== Uniqueness of identity proofs ==

'''Uniqueness of identity proofs''' (UIP) says that any two proofs of
<code>a = b</code> are equal. Streicher's '''axiom K''' is the special case that every
proof of <code>a = a</code> is <code>Eq.refl a</code>, and the two are equivalent.<ref name="hott">The Univalent Foundations Program, ''Homotopy Type Theory: Univalent Foundations of Mathematics'', Institute for Advanced Study, 2013; Notes to Chapter 1, Example 3.1.9 and §7.2. https://homotopytypetheory.org/book/</ref>
In Lean both hold by definition:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem uip {α : Sort u} {a b : α} (h₁ h₂ : a = b) : h₁ = h₂ := rfl

theorem axiomK {α : Sort u} {a : α} (C : α → Sort v) (h : a = a) (x : C a) :
    h ▸ x = x := rfl

#print axioms uip
#print axioms axiomK
</pre>

Both report that they do not depend on any axioms. The first is definitional proof
irrelevance: <code>a = b</code> is a proposition, so any two of its proofs are definitionally
equal. The second is what Carneiro calls K-like reduction: for a subsingleton eliminator,
proof irrelevance lets the major premise be replaced by the constructor, after which the
ordinary computation rule applies. For <code>Eq</code> this means that transport along
<code>h : a = a</code> reduces to the identity, whatever <code>h</code> is.<ref name="carneiro">Mario Carneiro, ''The Type Theory of Lean'', Master's thesis, Carnegie Mellon University, 2019; p. 4 (UIP and univalence), p. 12 (K-like reduction), p. 15 (proof irrelevance and axiom K in Lean and Coq). https://github.com/digama0/lean-type-theory/releases/tag/v1.0</ref>
Carneiro lists proof irrelevance and axiom K among the axioms commonly added to Coq, and
observes that they hold in Lean with no axioms.<ref name="carneiro" />

Homotopy type theory takes the opposite course. It reads a proof of equality as a path,
keeps proofs of equality relevant, and treats UIP as a property some types have rather
than an axiom.<ref name="hott" /> Its univalence axiom identifies equivalent types. The
two-element type then has a non-trivial self-equality, the swap, so the universe is not a
set, and univalence is inconsistent with UIP.<ref name="hott" /><ref name="carneiro" />
Because Lean's UIP is part of definitional equality rather than an axiom that could be
left out, univalence cannot be added to Lean without making it inconsistent.
